---
title: "Boundaries"
engine: julia
---

```{julia}
#| echo: false
using ConvolutionInterpolations, Plots, Printf
default(size = (720, 400), linewidth = 2, framestyle = :box, fontfamily = "sans-serif")
```

Near the ends of the data, a kernel's stencil reaches beyond the last knot: `:b7` combines twelve
values per evaluated point, so within six spacings of either end some of them do not exist.
Both packages fill those positions with ghost values extrapolated from the data, and the `bc`
keyword chooses how. The choice decides whether the interpolant keeps its full order up to the
boundary, and what it does when the data near the boundary are not smooth.

## The choices

- `:poly` extrapolates with a polynomial of the degree the kernel reproduces. For smooth data
  this keeps the full convergence order up to the boundary; it is the right choice whenever the
  data continue smoothly past the last knot.
- `:linear` and `:quadratic` extrapolate at lower order. They lose accuracy near the boundary
  on smooth data, but they do not amplify a step or a kink there.
- `:detect`, the default, uses `:poly` where the data near the boundary allow it and falls
  back to `:linear` where they don't, decided separately at each boundary. It also falls back
  when there are too few knots for the polynomial fit.

In Python the same options are strings: `"poly"`, `"linear"`, `"quadratic"`, `"detect"`.

## When it matters

Smooth data with a step close to the right end. Polynomial extrapolation continues the step's
steepness beyond the data and makes the interpolant overshoot between the last knots; `:detect`
recognises that the data there are not smooth and switches to linear extrapolation:

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Julia

```{julia}
xs = range(0, 1, length = 21)                             # 21 knots on [0, 1]
ys = sin.(3xs) .+ (xs .> 0.83)                            # smooth data with a step near the right end
t = range(0.5, 1, length = 801)                           # fine points on the right half

plot(xlabel = "x", legend = :topleft)
for (bc, style) in ((:poly, :solid), (:linear, :solid), (:detect, :dash))
    itp_bc = convolution_interpolation(xs, ys; bc = bc)   # the same data, three boundary conditions
    plot!(t, itp_bc.(t), linestyle = style, label = "bc = :$bc")
end
scatter!(xs, ys, markercolor = :white, markerstrokewidth = 1.5, label = "data", xlims = (0.5, 1))
```

## Python

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from convinterp import convolution_interpolation

xs = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 21)                            # 21 knots on [0, 1]
ys = np.sin(3.0 * xs) + np.where(xs > 0.83, 1.0, 0.0)     # smooth data with a step near the right end
t = np.linspace(0.5, 1.0, 801)                            # fine points on the right half

for bc, style in [("poly", "-"), ("linear", "-"), ("detect", "--")]:
    itp_bc = convolution_interpolation(xs, ys, bc=bc)     # the same data, three boundary conditions
    plt.plot(t, itp_bc(t), style, label=f'bc="{bc}"')
plt.plot(xs, ys, "o", mfc="white", label="data")          # the knots themselves
plt.xlim(0.5, 1.0)
plt.legend(loc="upper left")
```

:::

On smooth data the picture reverses: the polynomial extrapolation is the accurate one, and the
linear fallback costs accuracy in the boundary cells. The same sine, interpolated with `:poly`
and `:linear`, and the largest error measured in the two outermost cells on each side:

```{julia}
#| output: asis
xs2 = range(0, 2π, length = 41)                           # 41 knots over one period
ys2 = sin.(xs2)                                           # smooth data
h = step(xs2)                                             # the spacing
edge = vcat(range(0, 2h, length = 201), range(2π - 2h, 2π, length = 201))   # the outermost two cells on each side

println("| bc | largest error in the boundary cells |")
println("|:--|--:|")
for bc in (:poly, :linear, :detect)
    itp_bc = convolution_interpolation(xs2, ys2; bc = bc)
    @printf("| `:%s` | %.2e |\n", bc, maximum(abs.(itp_bc.(edge) .- sin.(edge))))
end
```

`:detect` matches `:poly` here, as it should: the data are smooth at both ends, so nothing
triggers the fallback.

## Per side and per axis

The boundary condition can be given per side, as a `(left, right)` pair, and in more
dimensions per axis, as a tuple of such pairs:

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Julia

```julia
itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y; bc = (:poly, :linear))          # polynomial on the left, linear on the right
itp = convolution_interpolation((x, y), z; bc = ((:poly, :poly),      # first axis
                                                 (:detect, :linear))) # second axis
```

## Python

```python
itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y, bc=("poly", "linear"))          # polynomial on the left, linear on the right
itp = convolution_interpolation((x, y), z, bc=(("poly", "poly"),      # first axis
                                               ("detect", "linear"))) # second axis
```

:::

## Outside the data

Everything above concerns points inside the data range; the ghost values exist so that the
stencil is complete there. What happens for a point outside the range is a separate choice, the
`extrap` keyword of the Julia package:

- `:throw`, the default, raises an error — the safe choice, since nothing outside the data is
  known.
- `:flat` returns the value at the nearest boundary.
- `:line` continues linearly from the boundary.
- `:natural` extends the data by the kernel's own extrapolation and interpolates past the
  boundary, so derivatives stay continuous across it. It extrapolates twice, which becomes
  expensive in higher dimensions.

```julia
itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y; extrap = :natural)  # evaluate a little beyond the data
itp(-0.1)                                                 # no error: extrapolated
```

The Python port does not extrapolate yet: points outside the data range raise a `ValueError`.
The [feature matrix](../features.qmd) tracks this.
